utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everybody. Good morning, Mr. McCloskey. I'm glad that you're here with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor Milincic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have just three short questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up in e-court 1D09746. This is your statement. I'm interested in paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Pay attention to the last two lines. I believe we have to go to the following page in the Serbian language. Are you familiar with this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next page, yes. Professor, is this your statement or is this somebody -- is this something that somebody put into your mouth?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very hard for anybody to put anything in my mouth. I'm a literature Professor. Marko Miljanov, a famous Montenegrin poet spoke about dignity and heroism and honesty. Honesty is to keep people from yourself and others from you. These are my original words. I always say that in everyday life, so nobody imposed words on me. I'm very sorry that somebody said yesterday that that was a copy, that I copied something from somebody. This is my original statement. This is the result of my reflections, my thoughts, my philosophy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now can we go to paragraph 16 in the same statement? Please read this paragraph as well. Are these your words, or did somebody suggest that you should say this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the situation in Srbac at one point in time when the situation was difficult and we tried to do our utmost amongst ourselves in Srbac, in my municipality, and across the Sava. There was the Croatian town of Davor. We tried everything in our power to avoid conflict, and there were attempts on both sides to conflict us, or we were shelled on three occasions from the Croatian side but not from our neighbour but from some other position, and they fully expected us that we would retaliate against that innocent town. And I personally, through my former student, the commander of my brigade, I asked him not to touch that innocent town and he listened to me and Davor was never sanctioned as a result of that. And since this was a very big news for Republika Srpska and Bosnia-Herzegovina, because we were shelled from the hideaway from Sanski Brod, the connections and communications were interrupted, and that evening you called me from home and you asked me about what had actually happened in Srbac, whether we were shelled, whether there were any casualties, and what was going on. And then I told you that, yes, we did have some damage, there were some casualties, some people were wounded, because the fire was opened and non-selectively. All over town there were some problems. It was very difficult to shell Srbac because it is protected by a hill, so those shells missed the main targets. We were shelled three times. On the first occasion, those shells fell on the Croatian side. That's why the villagers of Davor reacted. You called me that evening, at home, and I told you what the situation was. And you said, Well, beware of those who are trying to provoke you because the worse the situation the better off they would be. Talk to the Croatian side. Whenever you can, try to preserve balance in Srbac, but you do the same to preserve the balance between you and the Croatian side. Try to be as fair towards them as possible. Praise be lord we managed to preserve those good relations for five years. Every time you told me, Beware of those who are trying to provoke you, every time. And I must tell you that there were provocations from both the Croatian side and the Serbian side because somebody wanted us to start waging a war with the Croatian side but praise be lord we managed to thwart those attempts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Milincic, yesterday when you testified, did somebody suggest that you should say what you told us yesterday, or were those your words and what you knew?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to summarise everything that I said yesterday I may be tempted to change the style but the essence would be the same. Nobody can impose anything on me. These are my words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The interpreters are struggling to keep up with you. The strain on them is intense. There is no gap between questions and answers, and both you and Dr. Karadzic are speaking very fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll do my best. I'll try to slow down. As I said, if I were to summarise what I said yesterday, maybe I would change my style of speech because you can't step into the same river twice. However, the essence of my words, the points would be the same. I stand by whatever I told you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Milincic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender these two paragraphs, paragraph 10 and paragraph 16, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think you know my position on this, Mr. President. The Court has already ruled, so I won't repeat it as a general matter. I continue to consider it anomalous that this would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber allowed the accused to go paragraph by paragraph, but didn't say whether it would admit this paragraph or not. So if you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. I -- I -- then I'll just reiterate my position as quickly as possible. I went through the transcript yesterday and I noted first that Judge Baird had noted that if this had been tendered as a 92 ter statement, the information elicited yesterday would a fortiori have suggested that it would not be admissible and had to be led live. I also noted that when this exercise was proposed by Mr. Karadzic, the Presiding Judge indicated that it did not appear to be a useful exercise, as a general matter, and it would not be helpful to the Court in assessing the credibility of the statement or the witness's testimony. As a general matter, I think it is anomalous to suggest that when we don't know anything about the statement it's inadmissible because it's largely irrelevant, but once it's discredited then it becomes admissible. That simply is a proposition that I think cannot be used as a basis for admission. So that's our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To make it simple, do you agree to the admission of these two paragraphs or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't agree to the exercise. I -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You opposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I do oppose it, but I don't if the Court is minded to do it. I -- I -- again as with the other matters, I'm not -- it's not a matter of the statement itself. If the Court finds there is any assistance in having the words of these paragraphs before it, that's fine. I'm not trying to make a bigger problem. My issue was the larger admissibility question and that's what I concerned -- so for it's easier for the Court and the Court finds any utility in actually examining the words of the statement -- of -- of the paragraphs that the accused mentioned, I don't have a problem with that in -- in -- my problem is with the overarching principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. Tieger opened this door yesterday. He questioned him about a portion of paragraph 22, suggesting that because the witness's words were similar to words in another statement that what he was saying in his statement and in his testimony was somehow fabricated or suggested to him. We have now gone back and highlighted two paragraphs which deal directly with Dr. Karadzic so that they are the most relevant, and we want to show that his testimony that he gave yesterday as well as what was in the statement was, in fact, his own words and not those of our investigator; and, therefore, just as paragraph 22 was admissible for the Prosecution, paragraphs 10 and 16 are admissible for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson and Mr. Tieger, what matters here is not the -- is not the content of the statement but, rather, the fact that whether it was -- or they were the original words of the witness's or the result of some feeding up. So theoretically, the admission of the statement is not necessarily warranted, but in the circumstances where the accused did not read out the portion of the statement in order to understand the context of the witness, we will admit those two parts -- paragraphs of the statement, for that purpose only. We will assign a new number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit D4188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: He had concluded, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably I missed that. Well, Mr. Milincic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of this Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it next witness is ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's Colonel Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the next witness, I would like to make this observation once again. It's for Mr. Karadzic. The Chamber wanted to put it on the record that it is very concerned with how you are using the remainder of the 325 hours granted for the presentation of your Defence case. At the end of November, you had about 65 hours remaining. While it is within your discretion to decide how to best use your time, as long as you stick to issues of relevance to the indictment, the Chamber has already told you last week that it will not entertain any request for additional time. As long as this is clear, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I am not asking for any privileges because I'm an amateur but because the Prosecution filed 92 bis statements, and their number is 1500 -- or rather, 2500 -- and 2500 adjudicated facts and I have to deal with all of that, and herein lies the Prosecutor's advantage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Could the counsel assisting Mr. Blagojevic introduce himself for the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vladimir Domazet, from Nis, Serbia, counsel for Mr. Vidoje Blagojevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. As you may know well, Mr. Blagojevic, before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal. That is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony, compelled under such circumstances, would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd kindly ask you to pause between my questions and your answers, and could you please speak slowly so your words may be recorded. Did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up 1D49036.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention to the screen. Do you see your statement in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read the statement and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I read it and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we display the last page for the benefit of the witness so he may be able to identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement accurately reflect what you said to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you here today, would your answers to those questions be essentially the same as they are in this statement?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Essentially they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit D4189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read in English a short summary of the statement of Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic. [In English] Vidoje Blagojevic was a career military officer first in the Yugoslav National Army, JNA, and then in the Army of Republika Srpska, VRS. In July 1995, he held the rank of colonel and was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. Colonel Blagojevic received and issued orders in early July concerning the Srebrenica combat activities. He never received or gave any order for illegal activities and was not aware of any plan to commit crimes in connection with these combat activities. He had no contact with President Radovan Karadzic, and President Karadzic did not issue any orders to him or his brigade. Colonel Blagojevic was unaware of any plan to execute prisoners from Srebrenica. He states that the claim of Momir Nikolic that on the evening of 12th of July, 1995, Nikolic informed Colonel Blagojevic of the plan to execute prisoners is a lie. Colonel Blagojevic did not see Momir Nikolic on the evening of 12th of July. During the Srebrenica operation, combat activities, Momir Nikolic did not report to Colonel Blagojevic but acted under the direction of the Main Staff's security organs presents at the terrain. [Interpretation] At this moment, I have no questions for Colonel Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Blagojevic, as you have noted, your evidence-in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is through your written statement, in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Dr. Karadzic, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, it's been sometime. Can you acknowledge that you were convicted in this court under what was at the time known as count 3, murder as a crime against humanity; count 4, murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war; and count 5, persecutions as a crime against humanity; and count 6, inhumane acts which was defined as forcible transfer? Do you acknowledge your convictions for those crimes?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was unfortunately convicted in that trial but it was an unfair trial. It was an unfair process, for the following reasons: My right to defence was jeopardised. I did not have a defence in that trial. Also, during the proceedings, my elementary, my fundamental, right to a fair trial was violated. I'll give you just one example out of a series of examples that one would need to have a legal training for, is that I was not able to testify. My right to testify in my defence was violated. As I understand it, it could be incomprehensible to the Court but that's what happened to me. Perhaps later, if I have an opportunity, I can give you a short overview of how it impacted on the way I'm serving my sentence. If you have time, you will give me an opportunity to tell you about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Colonel. Colonel, it's your duty in this Trial Chamber to answer my questions. And you're always able to explain your answers. As you know, Dr. Karadzic will be able to ask you questions as well which may go to some of the areas that you're concerned with, but right now you need to answer my questions, okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And also please bear in mind it is a serious criminal trial against Mr. Karadzic. Please continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 6 --

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just complete my answer. You did ask me a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you answered the question, but if you'd like to add anything, please be brief, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be brief, but for my answer to be complete on the previous question, I just wanted to say that it was a kind of joint criminal enterprise by the Prosecution and the so-called defence which resulted in my conviction, and now I've answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were the victim here, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 of your statement you, in fact, say that it was Mr. Butler's report that violated your most basic right, and you referred to this, and the Trial Chamber -- and the Judges of the Chamber. And you say, and I quote: "Unfortunately this practice of torture and revanchism continued while I was serving my sentence." So I just wanted to add that that completes your answer to my question, I take it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload the statement? I'm not sure I have the most recent version. Is it paragraph 6, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I hope I have the -- I know there was versions being passed around. It's under the section "would you like to add anything else," the one that I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see such a paragraph in the statement. Can we upload it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think Mr. McCloskey may be working from a different version. The final statement was distributed to all of the parties after the proofing and that paragraph was deleted, or that language was deleted from paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this is the difficulty Mr. Tieger is confronting every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see that. Well, I think we've got this in the record, and I'll go on, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, do you feel that the -- do you acknowledge crimes were committed in Srebrenica but that they were committed by individuals and uncontrolled groups?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: On this issue, I can tell you this: Speaking of crimes, especially murder, I condemn every crime, especially killing, and particularly of vulnerable, unprotected victims such as women and children, or any person who does not represent a danger. My view is that the people who committed that, which is a violation of the law, should be prosecuted and punished. As far as Srebrenica is concerned, what really happened, I cannot be the judge of that. I can only speak about my unit, which was fully under my command, for which I was fully responsible and for all of its acts, as its commander. For all other cases, which went beyond my command, I cannot talk about them. I cannot say what crimes were committed, when, where, by whom. We may know more when this Tribunal provides a certain picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you believe the Srebrenica crimes were committed by individuals and uncontrolled groups? Do you stand by those words?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's a possibility. It's a possibility. Very probably. Because at that time, it was possible in that chaos for such groups and such individuals to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you think it's really possible that over 7.000 men and boys could be rounded up, detained, transported, summarily executed, and buried in a matter of four days, 13, 14, 15, 16 July, could that really have been done by individuals and uncontrolled groups? You're a military man. Come on. Give us some truth.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm an officer. I can tell you that considering that I had no knowledge about these things beyond the tasks given to my brigade, and which I endeavoured to carry out as best I could, abiding by the regulations that prevailed at the time over the army, I cannot be the judge of what happened outside of that. I cannot say whether something is possible or not. I have certain experience here, and I can tell you with what I know that what I thought was impossible did actually happen, so it is possible. It is not possible to make an efficient judgement or reason effectively without -- on the basis of speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 6, 5 and 6, the witness said that: What I thought was impossible turned out to be possible, rather than proved to be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's reflected in the transcript correctly. Please continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, roughly how many Muslim men and boys were detained in and around Bratunac on the 12th and 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean how many? You mean a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, this Court knows that your headquarters is right in Bratunac town. They know how small it is. They know all the schools where the prisoners were staying. They know a lot. And so I'm asking you: You were there, you had a front-row desk, how many?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not know that and I did not have an overview of the situation, did not have insight, and I just want to add to what I've said before. You would know better about these things if you had a military expert regarding the place and role of my brigade. The fact that there wasn't one leaves room for speculation. Of the so-called defence, I won't even speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, Colonel, let's go on. Let's go on. Let's go over what you may have known throughout some of the relevant time periods of this indictment that are related to Srebrenica which was the culmination of it. You've told us you started your career at the beginning of the war in the VRS, is that correct, in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what unit and where were you located in the spring of 1992? April, May, June?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Not April, May. Starting with 15 May 1992, that's the date when I reported to the command of the East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What town?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Ugljevik. That was the command post of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what job were you given?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was perhaps not so much occupied with a specific task but I was part of the operative section of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you become commander of the Zvornik Brigade of the East Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The corps command tasked me with trying to form the Zvornik Brigade as an organised unit, and I was there for perhaps two and a half months. That's perhaps from the end of May until, I don't know which exact date in July. I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if you were in the operations of East Bosnia Corps beginning in May in Ugljevik near -- not far from Zvornik and then you were trying to organise the Zvornik Brigade for the next couple of months, you were very present and on the ground during those days when Arkan and others arrived in the area, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you go -- you said you started at the Drina Corps when it was formed. You agree with me that it was formed November 1st, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe. I don't have the exact date. That information must be somewhere but I would need to be reminded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25558.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You can see under paragraph 1 of this order from the Main Staff, it's in the name of Ratko Mladic on the next page, talks about forming the Drina Corps from parts of the East Bosnia Corps, the Sarajevo Romanija, Herzegovina Corps from 1 November 1992. Does that help refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that in the first paragraph. I see what's written. It doesn't particularly concern me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've got to answer the question, Colonel. Does that refresh your recollection as to when the Drina Corps was started?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm saying I see that on the screen here, but to me it's just a piece of information. I don't know what else to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if you started at the Drina Corps the same time it started, you would have been working at the Drina Corps in November 1992?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. In November 1992 I was not in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when were you at the Drina Corps? Your statement said you started at the Drina Corps when it started.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It could have been in February or perhaps the beginning of March the following year. That is 1993. February, end February, or earlier March, I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6566, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the Chamber will rise just for a minute. --- Break taken at 9.55 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the remainder of this session and next session, we will -- we will be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to say this is the first time in the entire trial, I believe, that Judge Baird has not been with us. I don't recall any other time that he's been absent. We appreciate all the efforts he makes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we have Exhibit 65 ter 25789 on the board.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, this is a document we got from the Drina Corps archives that is something you'll be familiar with. It's a list of the duty officers for the Drina Corps, and it's for March - we can see that in the Serbian - 1993. And if you go midway down, go past Major Nedjo Blagojevic, down a bit farther, and you'll see a V Blagojevic. It looks like lieutenant-colonel. Does that help you remember that you were, in fact, in the Drina Corps acting in -- well, you were on the duty officer roster in March 1993, like you'd remembered?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. I agree. Whether it was the end of February or the beginning of March, but I've answered this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's just to back you up, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit P6567.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your job? We see "referent," referred to operations section. Can you tell us what position you held? You were a lieutenant-colonel. So in March of 1993, what was your assignment, what was your position in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was an operations officer in the operations organ, in the command of the Drina Corps responsible for certain tasks at the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of tasks?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I could name a few of them now; for example, preparing certain documents, reports, keeping certain records, duty service, participating in the making of the working map, and as required, getting involved in certain tasks according to the plan handed down by the command. I cannot tell you exactly. It depended on the situation on the ground and at the command. But my activities were mostly within the framework I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you got orders from your commander that were to go, be sent out to the brigade, did you sometimes help draft those orders and write them up so that they would go to the brigade in a proper format?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I took part in such situations at all, generally speaking. I was one of the desk officers. There were a number of desk officers assisting the chief of operations, and it all depended on what role he would give me. It depended on his decision. I never had a specific role.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was the chief of operations and training in March of 1993? Your direct boss?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have to remember now. At least two or three changed but I think I won't make a mistake if I say that at first, when I started, it was Colonel, at the time, and later on he was deputy commander in the Sarajevo Corps, Milosevic. He was a colonel at the time, I think, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would that be Dragomir Milosevic, who later on commanded the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think Dragomir, yes, that's right, yes. Yes, yes, yes. That's who I mean. But I think that after that, Lazic came. Now what was his first name, Milan? Was he a colonel? I cannot tell you exactly. Maybe Milenko, right, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in 1993, those first months that you were there, March, April, May, tell us how many people, how many officers, were actually in the operations unit of the Drina Corps? We know you had a commander and we know you, you call yourself a desk officer or we hear as a referent or admin officer, who else? What other officers were part of the operations unit?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you precisely right now, a military expert would have to do that for you and then you'd have a clear picture. Now, for me to try to get bits and pieces out of my head, what was there, what happened, I'd need a longer period of time to prepare but there were several officers who were in this operations organ. How do I put this? This is always a very strong organ within the command and the actual personnel changed. They would have other tasks, these officers, in the command, and so on. However, the intention was for as few as possible of them to stay on in the command. This were several of them, about ten, I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was Jocic one of them?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Jocic? I don't remember that last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You can't name one person, one other officer, that you shared your wartime offices with?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, sorry. Sorry. All right. All right. You said "Jocic" but I think it was "Jocic," Colonel Jocic, not "Jocic," "Jocic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Besides him, what other officers can you name?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The command [Realtime transcript read in error "commander"] of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I wanted the operations branch. But let's go on, if you can't tell me any.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, it was question in line 20, in the command, do you mean in the command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Unless you know any other officers in the operations branch, besides Jocic, you can't name anyone else of your wartime colleagues in the operations? Colonel, our records indicate you were understaffed and you had very few; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There were always very few people or there were not enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I want to show you a map graphic. It's Exhibit 65 ter 03205. It was something that the Office of the Prosecutor drew up, you may remember it from your trial.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean what I said just now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please. The interpreters didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, you mean unfair trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, this is just meant to give us some idea of the Drina Corps zone of responsibility which is in yellow. You don't need to really even read the English. And then we see the enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde, and this is for the time period 1995, and does that roughly fit your recollection as to the Muslim-held areas of the enclave in the Drina Corps in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe over here in my view, the factual situation on the ground was that these enclaves, Srebrenica and Zepa in a way, were linked up. Otherwise, that's it. The picture is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6568, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's all -- I didn't realise it's already an Exhibit P04941, page 6 of e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I just put this up here to get -- get that view of the Drina Corps in our heads, but now I want to go back to our chronology, back to 1993. By 1993, you would know that there was much larger areas of Muslim-held territory in the area of the Drina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The area was larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to a VRS map, Exhibit 65 ter 25786. And this is a map that we obtained from the Drina Corps. It's a VRS map. And hopefully our memories will allow us to see that this is the same basic shape as the map graphic that I had shown, and while it's not overly clear, up in the left corner we can see that there are dates up there, January 1, 1993, looks like 28 February 1993. Can you just for us, can you just read the Cyrillic up in the left-hand corner so we just know what this says?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Upper left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: "Work map of the staff. That's the work map of the staff, command of the Drina Corps. Beginning the 1st of the 1st, 1993. The 1st of January, 1993, and 28th of February, 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now if we could go back out a little bit, please, so we can see these blue areas. Now, you did say you took part in the working maps and while this is for the period just ending before you got there, can you tell us, these areas outlined in blue, is it the areas -- are those areas that were still held by the Muslim forces in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite possibly. This does correspond to the factual situation on the ground. I cannot strictly say yes now. But possibly it would correspond to the factual situation on the ground at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there were also thousands of Muslim civilians living in villages and towns within the areas outlined in blue, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were civilians living there but I cannot give you any relevant figures as to how many. But there were armed formations too, at any rate, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They didn't hear your end of the sentence. Could you say it over again?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that there were armed formations too, and then that can also be linked to the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And as the Drina Corps, it was their job, specifically the operations job, to know information for map drawing, for report writing, for order passing, to know about the armed formations; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Part of it is correct, but most of it is not exactly correct. Because it's not only the operations organ that takes part in the work of the command, many other organs do too and then all information is completed and then the final product is the final document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And correct. So as well as the armed formations, was it important for the command to be aware of the civilians, their numbers and their locations?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably for some structures in the command. Now, I cannot give you a strict answer to that question that you put.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For you, in operations, was it important to know where the civilians were and their rough numbers, especially as you have said they are associated with the armed groups?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: For me as an operations officer, it was important to know where the possible enemy objectives were, and that is to say units, and their combat resources. That was the danger for the army that I belonged to primarily. And that was the criterion for my involvement in that work primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where, if anywhere --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. McCloskey. Can I just clarify one thing with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Were these maps intended to be strategic maps or tactical maps? Both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, yes. The corps is an operative level of command so these maps were made at that level. They can be operative tactical ones too. However, they are not tactical, but at an operative level, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, I want to just ask you about where civilians fit in. You told me your main concern was -- the main threat was from the armed forces. Where, if anywhere, did the numbers and locations of civilians fit into your work?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Look, I have to repeat part of my answer again. Danger for me as an officer in the unit that I belonged to are the armed forces of the enemy, not the civilians. I'm just saying that. The armed units and their combat resources, their equipment. If I knew that, then I was okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you could -- once you knew that and you knew that threat and you could recommend commanders to take out that threat, that's what you -- that was part of your job?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I could give a recommendation to the head of the operations organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it may be naive of me but shouldn't you know where civilians are before you attack the -- what you believe are the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that civilians are an important thing to know about, but probably these civilians, due to their personal assessments with regard to their safety and security, et cetera, were at a certain distance away from these armed units, for different reasons. So the other side probably took care of that too. However, my knowledge of the deployment of the armed formations of the enemy is my primary task, and I, as an officer, cannot assume that there, where the armed forces are, or, for example, where an enemy nest was observed, from where a machine-gun was operating or another bigger, say, artillery piece -- I mean, if the enemy were to bring a number of civilians to keep them there in their immediate vicinity, no, that is unnatural, impossible, illogical. They have to be at a safe distance. I, as a member of the other side, took up positions and I aim at enemy targets. That's what I was taught at school. I cannot present any different kind of science now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, Colonel. I think you'll agree with me that we see this blue on this map and that by organised operations of the VRS, from the period where you were at the Drina Corps, and a bit before, engaged in these Muslim forces and defeated them to the point where the enclaves were created and the Muslims were restricted to the area of the map we just saw from 1995. Can you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so, you'll also agree with me, I think, that there are no more civilians left in these other areas, all the civilians were either in the enclaves or over in the rest of the BiH territory, Muslim civilians, that is; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, possibly. But I cannot claim with certainty where they went or where they -- I mean, or if somebody stayed on. I cannot claim anything to you with certainty, but in principle that would be it. It could be that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, there were no civilians left in the area of Eastern Bosnia of the RS except in those enclaves. You know that.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, now that I hear it from you, probably it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you a segment of a report of a UN rapporteur named Mazowiecki, who described the civilian flight during this combat that we've just spoke of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to Exhibit 65 ter 01219A? And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you mean to tender this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need to put it up? Marked for identification pending English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I can get some basic translations for the heading so that it's more useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 25786 gets MFI P6568, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I just want to briefly look at this front page, and it will not be my intention to offer this document into evidence. I think you have a shortened version of something similar. But I do want to ask you about some of its conclusions. We can see this -- who this is from, Mr. Mazowiecki, and it's first chapter is titled: "Ethnic cleansing of the eastern enclaves." And it gives the various places, Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Srebrenica, Gorazde and Zepa, and I'm sure you'll agree with me that those are the areas that were included in the blue marks, in part, that we just saw on the previous map. And if we can now go to the conclusion page, it should be page 18 in the English and page 19 in the B/C/S, and I'm concerned with paragraph 87, in part, which says: "Massive and repeated violations of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 were perpetrated in recent combat in eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina. These were cleared out by Serb forces in Cerska, Konjevic Polje and Srebrenica, and attacking and ambushing civilians attempting to flee their encirclement in attacking the villages themselves, in refusing to allow humanitarian aid to enter, in refusing to allow the evacuation of the wounded, in attempting to link the above issues to the independent question of freedom of movement for the Serbs in Tuzla." This document is dated May 1993. Also, if you look briefly at the next paragraph, it talks about violations of the Geneva Conventions of the other side by attempting to use these same civilians as human shields. So this report is giving a two-sided approach. Now, you are at the -- as you've told us, since March, are at the operations unit of the Drina Corps. Can you confirm that you received information of these violations of the Geneva Conventions against the civilians populations in these areas?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Not particularly, no. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't remember? So it's possible it happened, you just forgotten?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Quite simply I don't remember. If I don't remember something, that means that this information was not there, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the RS or VRS policy to force the Muslim populations in these areas out of these areas?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of such policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Wasn't this part of the orders of the Drina Corps, to take -- force the Muslims -- the Muslim population, out of these areas?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Show it to me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've seen it before, Colonel. But --

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this is an important matter, an important phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before I show it to you, tell us what you remember about the policy of your army, independent of any document. Let's forget about documents for a while. What's in your memory? Remember getting a highly illegal order to force Muslim population out of the area?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: What order are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm talking about your memory. Do you remember any such order?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Illegal? Unlawful?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P02085. And as you will see as this comes up, this is from the command of the Drina Corps, dated 24 November 1992, just before you arrive, and of course would have been applicable for the time period you're there. You will see that it's -- if you go to the third page in the B/C/S, it's in the name of your commander, Milenko Zivanovic. And it's the position of the Prosecution that this is directly related to Directive 4, which is P00976 under the name of Ratko Mladic, but I won't take the time. You may recall that document. And I would call your attention to this document, which came out of your command with a strictly confidential number 2-126. Perhaps you recall that the number 2 was the operative branch numbers; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, the first page.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry. There is the first page and we see the strictly confidential number 2-126. The numbers 2 at this point in time reflected they were from the operations branch; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's possible. I can't be sure about all the numbers, but it is possible that documents of this kind come or were prepared in the operations branch, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see in paragraph 1, General Zivanovic is telling the Zvornik Brigade and personally to the commander or Chief of Staff: Using the main forces and equipment and active combat operations, inflict the highest possible losses on the enemy, exhaust them, break them up or force them to surrender. Nothing wrong with that, is there? That's what you do in war sometimes?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it could be. I can't tell you. I'm not familiar with the document, but there you go. This is just to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a serious trial, Colonel. Don't just say something to say something. You've been called by Dr. Karadzic, especially on this question. What about the next part: And force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica and Gorazde? That is criminal on its face, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, a while ago, you had General Zivanovic here. Why didn't you clarify that issue with him? Why are you clarifying this issue with me? How can I tell you what was in his head, whether he had a criminal mind or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, take some responsibility. Take some responsibility. Answer the question. You were the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. You know what responsibility is. Answer the question. Is that criminal?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Please don't shout. I would ask you in the kindest possible way, don't shout. It has pierced my ears. I don't know about the others. I'm repeating. You had this man here. He could speak about other situations. He could tell you where things led and not ask me who -- I was in a totally different position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, Mr. McCloskey is not asking what Mr. Zivanovic had in mind. When you read this, do you agree that this sentence on its face illegal or criminal? That's the question from Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is how it may be understood, but I did not know what the commander's intentions were. I only knew what my task was, and I was the one who implemented the task and based my decisions on that. And now as to why somebody wrote this, it may have depended on the sequence of events. However, as I am looking at the document, I can't tell you whether there was a criminal intent behind it or not. It would show any -- a lack of any responsibility on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was it the practice of the Drina Corps in this operation to force the Muslim civilian population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica and Gorazde, as ordered by General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: On reflection, you have now made a link between Cerska, Zepa and Srebrenica, and the -- there was a time difference between the three. And those events did not have the same outcome -- or rather, the outcome of anything was not the result of operations that happened at different periods of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, please answer my question. Did the Drina Corps Brigade, did the Zvornik Brigade follow General Zivanovic's order here?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: As part of those forces, it seems that they did, they were part of the corps forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree. Okay. Let's go to 1995 now. Just want to show you one document to help us get a feel for your office in 1995. You were still in the operations and training branch of the Drina Corps in 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's see 65 ter 04243.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: While that's coming up, Mr. President, were you minded to take a break this morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course, please. I'm sorry, I'm a little confused on the break timing. Thank you for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 10 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, in looking at my outline I noticed I needed to come back to your convictions that I went over to clarify something, and that would be that, I'm sure you'll agree to me, that the convictions I mentioned for murder and persecutions were specifically related to the killings in and around the Vuk Karadzic school and did not -- you were acquitted on the broader charges on the overall murder operation and joint criminal enterprise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Essentially, if you look at the judgement, you could conclude that, but as to the events themselves, it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand. All right. We have gotten into 1995 now in our chronology and I'd like to show you a document, Exhibit 65 ter 04243, to help set the scene for us. In March of 1995, you're still working as an operations officer in the operations branch of the Drina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in March 1995, I was still in the operations organ of the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see this document that comes out of the Drina Corps command security department, interestingly under the name of Milenko Lazic, who is the chief of ONO, and that is operations and training branch; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, he was in that position at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As I think you mentioned earlier, he was one of your bosses, so at that time it's Milenko Lazic. And we see the only other persons aside from Lazic and yourself from the operations unit that's on this document is Colonel Predrag Jocic. Is that the person we were talking about before?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard you say "Jocic." That confused me a bit. But Jocic, when you say Jocic, I remember now, it could have been Colonel Jocic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And while the Trial Chamber has heard a bit about this operation Spreca, this document speaks for itself. You were obviously involved in some -- the documents relating to this operation, and I won't go any further than that. Is this a true and correct document, as far as you're concerned? Is that your signature there?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: This could not possibly be my signature. I don't know what it is. Look at it. There is no V, no B, nor anything that looks like these letters. This is unlike any variant of my signature. No way. The first letter here is P. Somewhere in the middle there is an M. It could be -- I don't know even if it's in Cyrillic or Latin letters, whether it's a P or "ch" in the middle. It's impossible that I wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you were familiar with the documents related to the Spreca operation? Again, which I'm not going to get into.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, if you could put to me some basic document to remind me, it's difficult to say anything on the basis of this. There is just the word "Spreca." It's a code name. That's how you recognise documents. I would need to see at least one basic document to remind myself of what it was about. This reminds me of nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does it help at least remind you that your chief, Milenko Lazic, was the chief in March 1995, as it's signed here?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Possibly, possibly. I don't question that. Does it say operative, chief of operations? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you remind me what "Spreca" means in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably we need the assistance of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Spreca, if I may help, is a name of a river that goes towards Doboj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My association is also with the river which exists somewhere in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6569, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in this early period of 1995, January, February, March, had the policy and practice of the Drina Corps towards the enemy that remained in the Drina Corps zone of responsibility, that is the 28th Division inside Srebrenica, and the Zepa Division inside Zepa and the Gorazde Muslim forces, did -- as far as you knew from inside the operations office, did your command have the same regard to the civilians inside those enclaves as they did to the civilians inside the blue perimeters that we saw on the map from 1993? Had anything changed from Directive 4 and the document we read?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: If I can speak about the Drina Corps as a whole, the attitude of the Drina Corps towards those enclaves, Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, was conditioned by the activities, military activities, emanating from those enclaves, or the rest of the front line which could have been connected with what was going on in the enclaves. It is my personal conviction that, as far as the civilians in the enclaves were concerned, the officers, at least I, did not have any attitude other than the normal attitude towards civilians, in view of the existing situation of course. We have to bear in mind there was a state of war. And in my experience as an operative officer, the treatment of civilians by the command was conditioned exclusively by the activities emanating from those enclaves, the military activities from the enclaves, or perhaps the broader area and the front lines there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 2, page 37, there was a whole subclause that is missing. It says: The attitude towards civilians in view of the existing situation, of course. And the subclause that is missing is: Leave them to live in peace. Let them live in peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said concerning civilians, let them live in peace, in the conditions, in the circumstances that exist, as dictated by the regulations, the international community, et cetera, but the civilians do not represent a danger.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Colonel Blagojevic speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, for the benefit of the interpreters, could you come closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In that question, I appeared to have heard you say something about the view of the civilians would be connected in some way to the -- to the Muslim army. Let me ask you this question, and maybe your answer can clarify it, and I'm sure you'll agree with me that March, April, May, June and even July, the 28th Division of the Bosnian army ran raids out of the enclave against the demilitarise agreement, killed Serb soldiers, attacked Serb villages, as part of a policy to tie down Serbian troops from the Sarajevo front. Now, given that was going on, all the way up to and into July, in that context, you, as an operations officer, would you feel that your army would be justified in taking down that army that's illegally coming out of the enclave and removing the civilian population? In that context that I described to you, would you feel justified in that context for your army removing the civilian population, that is with the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, if I understood the question, it refers to removing the population, the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't think that would be all right. I don't think that that would be a reason for my unit or the organ that I belonged to to do that, but I do think that because of the activities of the 28th Division out of the enclave against soldiers, civilians, et cetera, on the other side of that front line, in the depth, would justify activities of the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I'm not sure that there is an understanding between Mr. McCloskey and the witness is full concerning the -- translation, translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't follow you. You have an issue with respect to translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sounded to me like we agreed with each other and we were right on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue? If necessary, you can take up in your re-examination. Shall we continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Colonel, as I -- I take it that despite the context that I described that you agree with, it would still be improper militarily to remove the civilians. Let's go to another document, P03040, of the Drina Corps to see if we can look into the orders and the policies of the Drina Corps where you were working on March 20th, 1995. And we can see that this document dated 20 March 1995 is from the command of the Drina Corps. It is to all the Drina Corps brigades and units, and it's entitled, "Operative number 7."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I won't go into it, but it's the position of the Prosecution that this document is related to the well-known Directive 7 that came out in the name of Dr. Karadzic. And if we could go to the last page of the document, which should be 21 in the English and I have it as 10 in the B/C/S, just so we can see who it comes out under, we can see that -- 20 in the -- should be 20 -- well, you've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see that it came out under the name of the command -- the known commander, Milenko Zivanovic, and that it was drafted by Colonel Milenko Lazic, who we know at the time was the chief of operations. So we just saw you, Lazic and Jocic together. So this is a document that was created and drafted while you were in that office with these guys; right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember that particular circumstance, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to page 6 in the English and -- sorry, it's under the tasks of the Drina Corps in the B/C/S and I did not catch the B/C/S part of it. But it's -- we go to paragraph -- yes, you've got 2, the tasks of the Drina Corps, and you'll see it's down in -- not down far below paragraph 2, and it's the now very recognisable words that after issuing orders regarding various forces, Zivanovic says, drafted by Lazic: While in the direction of Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves complete physical separation of Srebrenica and Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves. By planned and well thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa. And this is directed towards the inhabitants of the Srebrenica and Zepa, is it not?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: You can conclude that from this text. I don't see what else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'm sure you recall this phrase from Dr. Karadzic's Directive 7, can you tell us whose decision it was who repeat this phrase from Dr. Karadzic's directive into Milenko Zivanovic's now order, taking it for directive to order?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe this will make you angry again but you should have asked the general, Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, don't worry, Colonel, I'm not angry. We are not angry. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: My answer is you should have put that question to General Zivanovic. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would General Zivanovic have any discretion when he receives a legal order from President Karadzic, when passing on that order to his subordinate commanders?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, General Zivanovic signed this document, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I am answering your questions. I'm saying this because General Zivanovic signed this document. Maybe this is an important question to which he could give an important answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on. You became the commander of the Bratunac Brigade on May 25th, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's go to a document about that, 65 ter 02082. And we now see a regular combat report dated 25 May, looks like it goes out sometime at 4.30 something on the 25th, in your name. When a document like this, a combat report goes out in your name, are you responsible for it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it's a combat report coming out of the brigade, basically it's approved, or rather, signed by the brigade commander or somebody standing in for him, if he's absent, but I don't see the signature of any other person here. However, the situation is a bit more complicated. But it's my document. What else can I say? Because it's possible sometimes that something is left out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see here that this reflects that you took over duties at 1000 hours. But I wanted to ask you, the first part says: Our forces did not open fire towards the demilitarised zone. And were you informed of when your forces shelled the demilitarised zone with mortar fire or artillery fire, as it appears in this document?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Not only that, that's something the commander should have issued orders for, it's a serious job, serious business, or somebody from the superior command, if they happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6570, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, I would think you would recall the communication and report that the -- a commander of the Bratunac Brigade from July 1994, Mr. Ognjenovic, communicated to his troops. And to refresh your recollection about it, it comes from P04075. It's 4 July 1994, from the command of the Bratunac Brigade, in the name of Ognjenovic. And on page 3 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S, he says: We must continue to arm, train and discipline and prepare the RS army for the execution of this crucial task, the expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave. There will be no retreat when it comes to the Srebrenica enclave. We must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible realising that they cannot survive there. Ognjenovic sent this out right after meeting with General Mladic. Did you do anything to countermand this communication, this report to the Bratunac Brigade troops, when you took over command?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: This document did not concern me at all. I didn't have it. I don't know what to tell you about it. It was one year before, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, this document was found in the archives of the -- the VRS records. I believe we got this from the Bratunac Brigade. It's our position this is an illegal order. Are you saying that an illegal order to expel the Muslims from Srebrenica done by a former commander would not be your business?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. You're saying that I claim that this is an illegal order?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the Prosecution's position that it's an illegal order.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Please be specific, Mr. Prosecutor. I'm not a historian. I'm a commander. I'm an officer. I got there, I was informed about the situation in the brigade, and I continued working as the commander in that brigade. I was not interested in history and what happened a year or two years ago. There was no time for that. Now, when the situation is calm, we can study history, because what happened at the time is already part of the history so we can study that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 04274. We are still on your first day at the Bratunac Brigade, 25 May. This is from the Drina Corps command, from Zivanovic, as you'll see, and it's to all the brigades of the Drina Corps and other units, and it's not exactly clear what time it goes out but I think if we look at some of the other documents we may get that idea. And we see here that it is informing all these units that NATO had carried out an attack at Jahorinski Potok, which were weapons warehouses, as you know, near Pale. And it tells all the brigades, in relation to this, and in order to take urgent measures to raise combat readiness of the PVO system to the highest level in order to take measures of the anti-aircraft protection and to protect the men, I order, and we can read paragraph 1 including the raising of the units of the highest level of combat readiness and the opening of fire shall be regulated by the Drina Corps through the Grabovica signals table. So did you, on this, your first day of command, get this order to -- informing you of the NATO bombing of that date, against your army, telling you to get ready to open fire?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Judging by the date, it seems that I should have received it and it was only normal for me to have received it because it is addressed to the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6571, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could now go to P04076.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, you'll see this is an interim combat report under your name, and this one we can see was at least delivered at 2110 hours on the 25th of May. It's to the commander of the Drina Corps, and I'll skip down to paragraph 3 briefly because under this you say that: We have taken steps in accordance with your order strictly confidential number 08/8-60 of 25 May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, for the record, I should have pointed out was the previous order we just saw from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
