utterances.text: So you, by 2110 hours, have acknowledged receiving that previous order and have taken steps in accordance with it. You also say that in accordance with an oral order from Colonel Lazic, is that the same Colonel Lazic, your former boss, the chief of operations and training of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that that's him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We fired at -- two shells from 105-millimetre howitzers, a total of four shells, on the town of Srebrenica at 1907 hours. Artillery observers at Pribicevac reported two shells fired near the Domovija feature. That's the Domovija hotel in the centre of Srebrenica town?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's possible. If my memory serves me well, the Domovija Hotel is in the centre. Srebrenica is not a big place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the other two shells, they don't know where they went, were not observed?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Look at the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Ah, first. [Interpretation] Yes, now I can see it. That's what I read, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, do you take responsibility for firing these howitzer shells on the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Partly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you mean "partly"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Because of what you read, pursuant to the oral order of Colonel Lazic. He was there. He represented the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. He shares responsibility from the Drina Corps, as did anyone that may have issued orders from the Main Staff, as is anyone from the Presidency that may also have issued such an order; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's not about sharing. It's about assuming responsibility. He assumes responsibility because he was there and he issued that order to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Good point.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was not my decision. It was an implementation of an immediate order. There is no two ways about it. It's very clear in military terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to Exhibit 65 ter 25799. Did you authorise any mortar shells to be fired at the enclave that day?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of anyone --

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember. I don't remember. I don't think so. Actually, I'm convinced that I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You didn't. Okay. Would anybody else have fired mortar shells on the Srebrenica enclave on that day outside your command?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: There were several units around Srebrenica. There were at least two other units on permanent positions. I don't know if anybody else was there in addition to them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Looking at this document, this is from the 28th Division, and this says at 1900 hours, which is, as we just saw, within a few minutes of the time you fired your howitzer shells, that two -- the Muslim army thinks that two 82-millimetre mortar shells fell near a primary school and killed one child and wounded another. You probably remember the ten-year-old, Jasna Gabeljic, who died that day? You're -- you know these things better than others. Can an 82-millimetre mortar shell get mixed up or be --

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... something, something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- confused with a 105-millimetre howitzer shell when it lands?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, let's clarify some things. I'm confused on some things, and I will ask you to repeat about those 82-millimetre mortar shells. Where were they? Can you take things one at a time, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a very simple document, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Colonel, perhaps we can put it very simply --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: What the Prosecution is asking is whether or not somebody on the ground could mistake the impact of a 105-millimetre artillery shell with the impact of an 82-millimetre mortar shell, in terms of identifying exactly what the weapon was that caused the explosion. That's the question you've been asked. Would it be possible to confuse the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm try to answer your question; however, I'm focusing on the document. I believe that this is not about Srebrenica but about the local commune of Suceska, and those are two entirely different geographical terms. I believe the distance between the two is 20 to 30 kilometres, and it is possible that mortar fire was opened there, but that has nothing to do with fire opened from a 105-millimetre howitzer. This is not even in the same sector. These are two different locations with a distance of some 20 kilometres between them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you read this report, Mr. Blagojevic? Could you read it out? And then I'll ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've not seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us know if you have done your reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm done reading. The doctor was in Srebrenica and the children were in Suceska local commune, as far as I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this refers to two places that were shelled, Srebrenica and Suceska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we know that they are right next to each other, just a few kilometres away. I think you've already said that. So can you go back to His Honour's question: Can one mistake a howitzer impact with the particular mortar impact we see here?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It is possible, but those who know would not be easily mistaken on that. However, confusion is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you'll recall, your unit lost track of two of your howitzer shells. They saw two land downtown Srebrenica and lost track of two at around the same time. So very likely, if not a certainty, that your two howitzer shells landed on Jasna Gabeljic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's not likely at all. It's just a speculation. And I would not go there. Artillery is more sophisticated than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, perhaps someone else fired at the same time. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer, I believe, that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6572, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go to 65 ter 25746.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, were you aware that shortly after 7.00 the same day that you fired upon this inhabited enclave with your howitzer, somebody else fired on downtown Tuzla and killed more than 66 young people gathered in the square? Surely you recall that.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I had no information whatsoever about that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to -- we see this UNPROFOR report, let's go to the next page in the English, it should be B/C/S page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I'm going to object to any questions about the details of this shelling. As you may recall during the Defence case, our expert prepared a report concerning this shelling which you excluded, and, as a result, we weren't able to produce any evidence about that. So I don't think it's fair for the Prosecution to go further than the fact that shells fell on Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This shelling, what did you mean by this shelling on Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: On the 25th of May, 1995, there was a shelling incident in the Old Town of Tuzla which is not charged in the indictment and which was the subject of detailed analysis by our ballistics expert. And having read that, you excluded and redacted that analysis, and we weren't able to present any evidence as to who may have fired that shell or the circumstances of it. So it's our position that it would be unfair for the Prosecution now to be able to elicit evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber hear from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Defence has chosen specifically to, of course, call Colonel Blagojevic, who, as the Prosecution's position is, that on his first day, he took part in a co-ordinated effort with the rest -- many other VRS units, at -- shelled all the safe areas except for Zepa. This goes to his involvement in these events, his knowledge of these events. This is a lead-up to the attack on Srebrenica. You've seen the document about making life unbearable. That is part of this historical context. When they call a man like this to defend the president, they open the door to his conduct that's relevant to the charged crimes, and especially joint conduct that you will see from later documents are occurring at the same time at a larger level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, isn't there a distinction between the technical aspects of the shelling in question and what this witness may or may not have known about them? The fact of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. And I was trying to make that distinction myself, but the document here is the former, so that's what I was trying to avoid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will allow the question. Please continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in the English, should be the next page in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And again we see this conclusion here, that as a sequel to air strikes administered by NATO, at the Pale ammo dump - it's our position that's the dump referred to in the VRS document we just saw - the BSA resorted to massive retaliatory shelling against Tuzla town and TAB which is considered deliberate targeting of the UN and the Tuzla safe area. The shelling commenced at 1910 hours, simultaneously at TAV and Tuzla safe area. Total of 31 impacts were recorded, up till 2100 hours. Out of these 13 impacted in and around - I won't go into all of that - one of them hit the old part of Tuzla city centre, a place where young people flock together, and, as a consequence, 66 people were massacred to death and 170 were wounded, amongst them 31 were critically injured. You know now, don't you, historically that a shell landed in the Tuzla centre killing at least 66 people and more at the same time you fired your shells; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, where which shell fell in that area that you are referring to, but I would like to add something to what you said. I would like one to be precise. This is an oral order in the presence of Colonel Lazic and that preceded the firing of the 105-millimetre howitzer. That should be borne in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. But do you agree that over -- that at least 66 young people were killed by that shell that evening? That's a Bosnian historical fact?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know of that case at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not my question. You know it shortly thereafter or now, don't you, to be true?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I hear that from you now, but at the time I was not informed and I did not know that somebody was carrying out any kind of operation or causing casualties on some side. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, I would offer just the first two pages of this, just to show you the time of this report and this incident. I don't think anyone is going to be contesting this incident in that respect, and the issue as to precisely who did it is secondary to my question, as I think you can tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's been read out, Mr. President. So I don't think there is a need for the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We tend to agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the 66 people deserve more than a reading out. This may be the only record, and I would like it to be in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: But it is in the record, Mr. McCloskey. It's in the trial record, together with the timings and your observations of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you're happy that my reading is just as good as the document, I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will not admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, let's now go to 65 ter 19281. This is another May 25th document from Mr. Akashi to Kofi Annan. And in it notes just in the first paragraph, that: After the air strike of 25 May 1995, all the safe areas, less Zepa, have been shelled and the Bosnian Serbs have fired heavy weapons from five weapons collection points around Sarajevo. I won't go on and read the rest. So did you become familiar in the days and months after this that, in fact, the day that you fired your shell on -- your shells on Srebrenica, that the other safe areas had also been fired upon in --

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6573, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I note that my time is up. I do have probably 30 more minutes. Do I not intend to rehash the events of Srebrenica, but I do want to finish up this particular area of questioning and some Srebrenica events, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Usually we do not limit -- usually be lenient, but today we have -- really pressed with time. General Tolimir is going to appear today, according to our subpoena decision which specifically indicated today is the day he should appear. And I'm not sure how much time Mr. Karadzic would need for his redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, General Tolimir is here, as is his legal adviser. I would suggest we just suspend the examination of Colonel Blagojevic and call General Tolimir. I think we will be able to conclude him by 12.30 and then we will be a little more relaxed for time for the rest of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's a very good idea. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, do you follow? Do you understand what we just discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. It is clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much time would we need to prepare the setting, change the setting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will rise just for three or five minutes. --- Break taken at 12.10 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, we are now in full Bench. Good afternoon, General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Would the counsel assisting Mr. Tolimir introduce himself for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm Aleksandar Gajic, and I'm legal adviser to Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Gajic. Mr. Tolimir, as you may know well about this, before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that your answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony, compelled under such circumstances, would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TOLIMIR
utterances.text: May God be with you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: God be with us. But I'm asking you to kindly pause between my questions and your answers as well. In order to avoid any confusion from triple interpretation, because my notes are in English, with your permission and with an apology that is due, I'm going to put questions to you in English and I hope that the interpretation will be accurate. [In English] Can you tell us what positions you held during your military career?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question? The first part of your question was overlapped with the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what positions you held during your military career?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I started my military career in 1971 after I completed the military academy. First of all, I was a squad leader or a platoon leader in Slovenia during manoeuvres. This was a military exercise in the then-army. Then I was reassigned to Skoplje. From Skoplje, I was deployed in Titov Veles. I stayed in Titov Veles until 1975. And I commanded a platoon, a company, a squad, and so on, different basic units, if you will. In 1984, I was sent to the school centre of the Yugoslav People's Army in Pancevo for a course for security officers. After that one-year course, I was returned to Titov Veles yet again, and then practically carried out these duties that I had been taught; namely security organ in that regiment, 212th Regiment, where I served in Titov Veles. After that, I was assigned to the duties of security organ for practical training in the military naval district and I was a desk officer there at the security organs until 1980 something, 1986 maybe. And then I was appointed assistant head of that counter-intelligence group. That was a group that was involved in intelligence and counter-intelligence, counter-intelligence of foreign forces and armies against the Yugoslav People's Army. Then I was sent to the high military and political school, I think that was sometime in 1980. The school went on for two years. We graduated from that school, and after I graduated, I was returned yet again to this unit where I had been before that, in the military naval district. I assumed the same duties. After that, I was sent to a course sometime in 1986, a foreign language course. I studied Russian there officially. And sort of, by the bye, I learned English, sort of optionally. After I completed that course, I was returned to the duties that I had before that in Split and at the military naval district. After that, I carried out those duties again, the deputy head of this military naval district. Thank you. After that, I was sent to another garrison, Knin, where I was appointed head of the security organ. Then after Knin, I was sent to the war college in 1991. That's when the war was going on in Croatia. Then they returned us from that war college. We all had to go back to our units because the war had started. After that, I was seconded to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of the Serb Krajina, until, say, March of 1992. After March 1992, I was assigned to some duty there in that organ, at the time that was a transition period for the military, for civilian structures and everything in the Republic of the Serb Krajina. After that, after the 12th, around the 20th of May, 1992, I was assigned to the 9th military district. That was the Sarajevo military district. Actually, yes, yes, that was it. The 9th military district in Sarajevo. And after that, I was assigned -- well, when they asked whether we would go to Yugoslavia or whether we would -- I stayed in Republika Srpska then because I was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that's where I completed elementary school and high school, in Glamoc. That is roughly what I can say, sort of off the cuff. If I skipped something, you can ask me, if you're interested in something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General, sir. Can you tell us. [In English] What was your position in the VRS in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My position in July 1995 was assistant commander for intelligence and security affairs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever inform me, either orally or in writing, that prisoners from Srebrenica would be, were being, or had been executed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. President, as far as Srebrenica is concerned, the only time I spoke to you was on the 9th of July, 1995. I believe that it was on the 9th. And then I shared with you the information that was received by the Main Staff and that was that the Army of Republika Srpska was coming to Srebrenica. There were no prisoners at the time. And then you said that if they could take Srebrenica, they should. I drafted a document to that effect and I sent it to the units and to the Main Staff for their information. I told them that you ordered that they should be mindful of the civilians, UNPROFOR and prisoners of war. However, at that time there were no prisoners of war. And that was my last contact and conversation with you regarding Srebrenica and the situation there. Later on, I was deployed -- I was appointed assistant commander in Zepa, which is 20 kilometres away from Srebrenica. There are no communications between the two. And I did not communicate with you again because I was not in a position to know anything about those events, so I can't say anything about the ensuing events, because when we spoke there were no prisoners and I could not inform you about something I didn't know or see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Exhibit P2989 is the log of the republic communications centre in Pale for July 1995. It shows that reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It shows that reports were received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second. Just a second, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So I believe we would need 14th, 15th and 16th and 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What page should we go?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I'm not able to tell right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking for that, Mr. President. We have intended that this only be -- this reference be for the parties, but if we could look through the document, if I could look through it for a minute, I think page 5 will be the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if Mr. Tolimir could follow without seeing these notations or record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. If we could just direct General Tolimir's attention to page 5 and counting up from the bottom, there is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and that shows an entry that we are interested in as well as the two underneath that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, do you understand what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I can see here where it says the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is too far from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you speak to the microphone, if you could, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. On line 5, I can see where it reads the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and in brackets, OB. This is an abbreviation standing for security organ. The document is sent to the president. This is a piece of intelligence. At that time, I, not me but my organ, sent to as many as 20 different addresses. You will find those addresses in the document. And a document of this kind will contain all kinds of intelligence on what was going on in the world and that concerned Republika Srpska. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So I will continue in English. It shows that reports were received from the VRS security and intelligence organ and transmitted to the president, Ministry of Defence, and the state security of the Ministry of Interior of those dates, for 13, 14, 15, 16, 17th of July. These reports cannot be located now. Did any of them contain any information about the execution of prisoners from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, I don't know what those reports contained because those reports were drafted by the security organ, which was at the command post at that time, and I was in Zepa; thus, I don't know. If I were to see the original of those documents I could see who signed it, who processed it, at what time it was dispatched and to whom. These are the addresses, the 20 addresses that I mentioned, to which such documents were customarily sent. This should also include the minister of foreign affairs, who participated in international negotiations. I don't know what those documents contained, because I didn't author them. I was in Zepa. If the Presidency doesn't have this document, then you should refer to one of the 20 addresses to which the document was sent, the 1st Corps, the 2nd Corps, the 3rd Corps, and so forth. The Prosecutor could have found that document in any of those addresses. We ourselves could not do it. And thank you, Mr. President, this is as much as I can say about the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, I have no further questions for General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bear with us a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Tolimir, you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, but in the meantime, there is a scheduling issue. We haven't concluded the cross-examination of Mr. Blagojevic. So we'll ask you to excuse yourself --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But Mr. Tieger and I have had a chance to discuss this and this very basic information. We don't really feel a need to cross-examine on this situation given the entire context, unless Your Honours would like me to, based on this information. I -- we, Mr. Tieger, is satisfied that we've had enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Tieger. General Tolimir, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber I would like to thank you. You may be excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to thank everybody present, Mr. McCloskey, President Karadzic, the entire staff, and the interpreters. And may these proceedings finish as God wishes and not as I wish and may God's peace be with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gajic, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we bring in Mr. Blagojevic again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: How about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm carried away. Thank you. We will break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.25.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I just want to remind everyone we do have to finish Colonel Blagojevic today because his counsel is not available after today. But now we have what should be plenty of time, but let's not get carried away either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have to bear in mind that there is a swearing-in ceremony today in this courtroom, so we have to withdraw ourselves at least by 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That should be enough for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we have 65 ter 25792, up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, we will be done soon, but I have a -- this is a map graphic and I know you're a Bosnian and know this area well, as all Bosnians do, and can you confirm that where these red stars are are the places where those -- those UN protected enclaves were, Bihac, Tuzla, Sarajevo, Gorazde and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there is a document that's in evidence in the case that I'll show you a bit, that talks about going from Banja Luka to Pale. And we can see -- can you tell us, driving a car in that time period, obviously if an officer or the president was driving from Banja Luka to Pale, they wouldn't go through the federation. Can you tell us roughly how long it would take to drive from Banja Luka to Pale, just very roughly, in those days, May, June 1995?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you only roughly. I can't tell you with any certainty because, first of all, until Bijeljina, which is somewhere halfway, you need five, six hours, maybe more; and from Bijeljina, which is in the middle roughly speaking, to Pale, you would need another five or six hours, but that's driving without any stops. And it all depended on the conditions on the road and whatever you had to do on the way. It takes a lot of time, more than half a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6574, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have P02781.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, this is the document I mentioned. It's from the CJB in Banja Luka and it's just talks about Dr. Karadzic's movements and as well as chairman Krajisnik travelling from Banja Luka to Pale. And we can see here that on the 25th, it says that he left at -- they left at 1300 hours. And then we see this little scratch up in the right-hand corner, it says, arrived safely, 2220 at Pale. So my math tells me that's about nine, nine hours and 20 minutes. Is that -- was that -- would that be consistent with driving, if you're the president?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't put myself in their shoes. I can't answer this question. It would be pure speculation. I just can't give you a rational answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, it's roughly consistent with what you just said. You said around 10 hours. This is about 9 hours and 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said more than half a day, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. One last document on this topic. Could we go to 65 ter 16502. And you'll see that this is from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and I'll just tell you it's in the name of General Milovanovic, and it's dated 25 May. The actual time is hard to make out, but I wanted -- as we look at that first page at the bottom, we can see that in the Sarajevo -- this is a -- a report, excuse me, from the Main Staff, from Milovanovic, to the president of the Republika Srpska and the commands of the corps, as the Trial Chamber has heard about these reports in detail. And we see when we look at the section regarding the Sarajevo Romanija Corps down at the bottom, and it should be as well there on your page, that the president is informed that overflights of NATO aircraft, that NATO fired from the NATO aircrafts using air bombs against the area of Jahorinski Potok over the warehouse, and it explains that damage. And then it goes on in page 2 of the English, should be on your page still, says: Situation, under situation in the corps, all corps units are at the first level of combat readiness for shooting the goals in the air space. It says: Artillery was used against selective targets, the repeater hum, UN check-points, except the Russian one. Do you have any problem with -- is there anything wrong, in your view, with the VRS targeting UN check-points after NATO targeted VRS ammo dumps?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a judgement call of the person who had the right to make the decision. What can I tell you? In that situation, the decision-maker had more information, a broader picture, and had more material to make the decision. I don't know what he was guided by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "who," who do you mean? Mladic or Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person who made the decision. I don't see who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That would be at the highest levels of government, though, wouldn't it, army or government?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it here. Maybe I didn't follow closely enough what you've read, but I didn't see who gave the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the Drina Corps area of this report. It should be on page 4 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. And here under section B, situation in the corps, we see artillery was used against the enclaves, Srebrenica and Gorazde and Tuzla airport. So in this case, the president is being told of the -- your shelling of Srebrenica; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This could be connected with what we've just discussed, the order I received from the superior command. It was carried out in the presence of the representatives of the superior command. Yes, the two could be connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6575, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, one last set of questions on one document, and I'll let you go on to the next questioner. If we could go to P05074. Colonel, you will probably remember, this is an intercept from 15 July 1995, and in the Prosecution's case and under the evidence in this case, it was between Colonel Ljubo Beara, who we know to be the Main Staff chief of security, and General Krstic, who at the time was the commander of the Drina Corps and engaged in the Zepa operation. And we can see here that Beara tells Krstic: General, Furtula didn't carry out the boss's order. Krstic says: Listen, he ordered him to lead out a tank not a train. Beara: But I need 30 men, just like it was ordered. Take them from Nastic or Blagojevic. I can't pull anything out of here for you. I won't read everything. It goes on. And, finally, Krstic says again in the middle of the page: I'll see what I can do, but I'll disturb a lot. Have a look down there at Nastic's and Blagojevic's. Beara says: But I don't have any. If I did, I wouldn't still be asking for the third day. Krstic: Check with Blagojevic. Take his Red Berets. So, first of all, Radomir Furtula, who is that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You remember the -- the commander of the Visegrad Brigade? He was part of the Srebrenica operation, I believe.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there should be a rank next to his name. This way, Radomir Furtula could be anyone with that name and surname. I don't know. If there was a rank next to this name, maybe I would remember. This is too arbitrary. I cannot speculate. Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not asking you, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- all we see here is Furtula, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And my question is: Was there a Furtula who was the commander of the Visegrad Brigade when you were commander of the nearby Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not really nearby, Mr. Prosecutor. It's at least 80 kilometres away. And second, if you tell me his name, surname and rank, I can answer. But if you tell me just Furtula, I don't know which Furtula you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Lieutenant-Colonel or Colonel Radomir Furtula, ever heard of such a person?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, he was -- or rather, there was a Lieutenant-Colonel Furtula, one brigade commander. I don't know if you know a colonel by that name. But there was Lieutenant-Colonel Radomir Furtula, one of the commanders. I don't know exactly which. There were three or four of them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So we've got that. Now, do you recall the name of the commander of the Milici Brigade, which is very close to you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were my neighbour on the left, in a defence position facing Srebrenica enclave. I believe at that time, it was a certain Lazic. I can't be sure because they rotated them very often in that period, or perhaps it was another person. You have to help me. There was a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Nastic?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nastic, Nastic, that's it. Thank you for your help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do your remember his first name? I can't remember it off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it Milan? I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Rank? What rank was he?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps major. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you have a unit known as the Red Berets at that time in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit Red Berets did not exist in the wartime brigade. That name was given earlier, before I joined the brigade, but the men from that unit who continued to be called Red Berets were assigned to the 3rd Battalion of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. Rade Petrovic, I think, was its leader?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rade Petrovic, yes, son of Sreten Petrovic, yes. He kind of imposed himself as their commander, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you -- do you remember the member of the Red Berets unit that was wounded sometime after about 5.30 p.m. at Kravica on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any reports about that at that time. It was later, when I was already here in the Detention Unit, looking over some materials, that I read it in a document, but that's a piece of information that is of absolutely no assistance to me. I only read that in -- in that document. I don't even know what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So then back to this intercept, are you the Blagojevic that General Krstic is sending Colonel Beara to? And let me ask you, this is your chance to tell us something important: Did Colonel Beara come to you on the 12th, 13th, 14th, 15th, 16th of July, any time during that time, and request of you any assistance for the work he was doing?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He was in your brigade, wasn't he? Present at your brigade during those -- some of those days?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You saw this guy?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't -- no, he didn't -- I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've seen him before, he's about 6-6, 250, 280, big shock of blond hair? No, never?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was just going to mention that these American measurements of feet and pounds probably won't mean too much to Colonel Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know how they translate it. I don't know if they do the centimetres. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Two metres and 120 -- 110 kilos, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm just remembering the scales from my last trip to the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes or no? No Beara? Yes Beara? Think about it, Colonel, and it's the last question.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never measured his height or weighed him, that's one; and second, I never saw him and he never was in my brigade, nor did he ever contact me or approach me. Never at that time. Please remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not much, your Excellencies. I have some but not much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, on page 53 you were asked -- or perhaps a bit further down, you were asked about the decision to open fire and you said it was up to the person who made the decision. Can you tell us who made decisions for a unit under attack to respond, and does a unit under attack wait for approval from the president or anyone else to open fire in return?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning that situation, as I imagine it, I can tell you very simply. If a unit is attacked, it has to respond with all possible means to save itself and its men. So the decision in that case is made immediately in that situation by the commander of the unit under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was suggested on page 53 and it was read out to you that in a UN telegram, it said that Serbs shelled Muslim enclaves after NATO air strikes. So on that day, on the 25th of May, and later on, on the 25th of June, were there any actions launched from the enclaves against Serb territories?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that date, there had been very important military activities that were creating a serious military situation, and raids were run out of the enclave against villages outside the enclave and there were ambushes set. I can tell you of at least two or three cases, there was one village which was in the area of the neighbouring Milici Brigade and the second ambush with numerous fatalities was just between the left flank of my brigade and my left neighbour, which was the Skelani Battalion, and in that ambush one van was ambushed and a lot of men were killed. There were also a lot of sabotage actions, and it was typical. Those contact mines were set. The contact mines can easily be moved and when you step on them, or when a vehicle runs over them, they are activated. I had numerous such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where did those sabotage men come from, these terrorists?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned those places, and those troops were identified very close to Srebrenica enclave so my conclusion was, and it was only logical to conclude, that they came from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 45, it was suggested to you that you had fired four shells on Lazic's order and that they landed on the town of Srebrenica. Did you fire them on the town of Srebrenica? Were there any legitimate military targets in the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I answered that question just a while ago. As for that action that was carried out, I was safe in that action because I was in the presence of the officer from the superior command, from the corps command, who was in touch with the observers. Those were artillery observers who were deployed in the vicinity in order to observe military targets that may have posed an immediate threat to our troops, and he's the one who requested the opening of fire so the only thing that I can see is that the target was a military target, that it could have been a command post, and that's why action was ordered by that officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the interpreters understood when you said the "Domovija." What is Domovija?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Domovija. I believe that before the war, Domovija was a hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It says in document P6570 that the objective was to expel Muslims. Does that imply Muslim civilians or Muslim armed formations?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my deep conviction, as an officer and as participant of the events that took place at the time, that the main objective was to subjugate the enemy. And as for the civilians, according to all the conventions and laws regulating the matter, they should have been treated differently, without any force and the application of force. I can't say anything about the decisions made by the enemy with regard to their own civilians, whether they took the civilians with them. It would be speculation if I said anything. However, my position with regard to the military actions, they should target only the military elements, i.e., the military formations of the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When -- pursuant to the provisions of the international rule of war, is it inadmissible to make the life of the enemy unbearable? Is it allowed or not allowed?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: When you say the enemy, you imply a military force. And it is absolutely allowed. However, I would like to refer again to the innocent part of the population which does not pose a direct threat. This is obviously out of the question and this is my position. That was my position at the time, and that's the rule that I complied with in my command of the unit. And that's why I said at the beginning that I would sincerely hope that the Trial Chamber will allow me to say something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are on my time, so I can give you that time.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean I can say something else? I'll try and be very concise and brief and up to the point. I don't want to go over the same ground again. What was the problem in all that? I have to say this: I did not have defence. I was on my own in this courtroom. I suffered for a year and a half. I did not -- I was not allowed to say anything. I did say a couple of things when I could no longer sit still because I was going crazy. I was not -- I didn't dare say anything because I thought that everything would turn against me, and it was turned against me. But my conscience is clear. Things were done unbeknownst to me. And the joint criminal enterprise that was so portrayed by the Prosecutor, was supported by the so-called lawyer who was in charge of my defence, although he wasn't. I'm sorry, I become very excited when I speak about this. If -- things continued when I was in prison, in Trondheim, in Norway. There I received some illegal decisions which resulted from the violation of the national criminal code. I'm here to fight that. So far, my fight has been futile, but it hasn't stopped. On one occasion, in the evening, although they know that my eyesight is impaired and I can't use my right eye, they tried to give me a tablet which was very, very small, black but very small. Luckily enough I spotted that tablet among --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This goes well beyond the scope of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I didn't know what the Colonel would be telling us, although I understand that his emotions are running high. I will continue with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here on page 39, you heard the term "removal of civilians." In our language, what connotations does the term "removal" have? How did you understand the term "removal of civilians"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a human being, I can understand that this means to help them to move out or to be resettled. That's how I can understand this. However, I'm telling you if one starts -- started wondering how that term came about and what caused it, then I can't be absolutely certain because the enemy side may have had a lot of influence in that. One has to see what the decisive influence is from one case to the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How could the enemy side have influenced all that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, it could have influenced the situation by imposing ideas and pursuing different policies, but that has nothing to do with the military principles and the decisions made by officers. It is other people who do that. It does not pertain to my manner of commanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does our own national legislation regulate obligations towards one's own civilians and the enemy's civilians in the area of combat activities? What is an enemy -- what is a military force duty-bound to do when it encounters civilians on its path?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position arises from what I learned about the rules and regulations that I was duty-bound to comply with. And that means that we were duty-bound to protect civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the situation. If nothing else was possible, if you didn't have other means, and I mean if you didn't have food or medicines or anything like that, then at least you had to move those civilians from the area where there was combat going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. I'm asking this because -- in order to check whether there is a transition issue. Mr. Blagojevic, you said a minute ago - let me find it: The removal of population means something to help the population to move out or to be resettled. Do you remember having answered so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant was that they should be protected, that they should be moved from such places where they could become collateral damage, where they could be hit. This is what I meant. So if that was within my purview, if that was something that I had to decide on, that would have been my position, to move them somewhere safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On page 74, line 20, Mr. Karadzic, when you asked Mr. Blagojevic about the term "removal of civilians," what verb did you use in B/C/S for "removal"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, in the cross-examination, the term removal was translated as "uklanjanje" or "ukloniti." In our language, this term has a lot of connotations. That may also mean to kill the enemy. This is the term that I used, "ukloniti."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that term identical to the one that was used in Drina Corps document, i.e. Exhibit P3040? Drina Corps order, operation number 7. So this could be answered either by the parties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. "Ukloniti" was not used in that document. It was something else, "take out," "move out," but the word "resettle" was also not used because resettlement implies permanence to move people somewhere forever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave it at that. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked on page 33 whether the Drina Corps implemented Directive 4. Did you have any information as to what the Main Staff had in mind about whether Directive 4 had been implemented or not? If not, just say so. Did you know what the position of the Main Staff was with regard to the implementation of Directive 4?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have an insight into that so I cannot answer your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 09219.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just to answer your question regarding the Drina Corps document, P3040, that's entitled, "Operative number 7," it's that language that you'll recall: By planned and well thought-out combat operations, create an unbearable situation with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants. So it's not talking specifically about removal. That would be the -- Directive 4 goes more into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Combat order, operational number 5, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the first sentence, or rather, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Since the Drina Corps forces did not execute their task from Directive 4, the enemy switched to counter- offensive in the eastern part of the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps and succeeded in inflicting large losses on the units of the Drina Corps in Glogova mountain, in the general area of Bratunac, Skelani and Rudo. The attack against Visegrad is ongoing."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you also read the last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The civilian population should not be destroyed. It should rather be allowed to move to other areas, or if they accept the authority of Republika Srpska, they should be disarmed and the Serbian civilian authority should be established."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Serbian version as well, we need the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you now look at paragraph 4? Usually this paragraph is a decision and after Srebrenica, Skelani, can you read to the end?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In co-operation with the forces of the Drina Corps, break and destroy the enemy forces in the general area of Srebrenica. Liberate the Sase and Kunjaci mines and cut off the green transversal in the general area of Srebrenica, and then in co-ordinated action with the Drina Corps forces, embark on the gradual destruction of the enemy in the general area of Zepa and Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this imply the destruction of Muslim civilians? Is there a single officer, or was there a single officer in the Army of Republika Srpska who could construe this as an order to destroy Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see this as a destruction of Muslim civilians. This is combat and trying to defeat the enemy force under arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit D4190, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no time to deal with the document that Mr. McCloskey mentioned, 03040. It has been admitted, so we will eventually come to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you -- you were asked on pages 15 and 16 whether you knew about what was going on in the town of Srebrenica itself. Where were you during the night, actually, from the afternoon of the 12th until the morning of the 13th?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The afternoon of the 12th until the 13th in the morning, that is the first day after I returned to the command of the brigade. And after that work-day I went to the Fontana Hotel, quite simply to refresh myself, to get some rest and to renew my capacity to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you receive information from someone in terms of what was going on in town, or did you tour the town itself that night?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you well informed about what was going on and about the neighbours along the line where your brigade was? I mean, not your own brigade but the neighbouring ones. Actually, the situation on the front.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I was informed to a necessary degree so that I could command my unit in the way that I considered to be optimal at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 02105. It's on the next page. It's handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, is this your handwriting, or did you dictate this to someone?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what can I -- well, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can go back to the first page in Serbian so that the witness can see this typed up on a teleprinter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly somebody was typing this up at the operative organ. I don't know. I'm not 100 per cent sure because of this signature. It's illegible so I cannot quite decipher it with certainty. Can you change this? Can I see the other part that was written?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean the next page?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Is there a signature here, down here? Well, that is what confuses me. I do not see that that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is this document about, regardless of whether it's one of your co-workers or you? Why is it important to know where your forces are on the left flank?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is important because of linking up with the neighbour to have a certain link, I mean contact, I mean for the control of that mutual link-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the learned Mr. McCloskey said to you, do you agree, do you accept, that 7.000 men and boys were executed in Srebrenica, according to what you know now, what you learned subsequently, in Srebrenica itself, and in the territory of the municipality of Srebrenica, was there an execution there? I'm not asking you what you knew then. Did you hear later where that happened?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know then. I don't know now. I know nothing. Maybe you find that incredible but you asked me about the territory of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes the municipality of Srebrenica, the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know a thing, I really do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, sir, Colonel, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit D4191, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence, Mr. Blagojevic. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to the Tribunal again to give it. Now you're free to go. Our thanks also goes to Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I would also like to personally thank Mr. Domazet because he appeared for Colonel Blagojevic on a pro bono basis, and I think he exemplifies the very finest of the profession to do something like that, and I thank him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we going to hear the next witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the next witness is Sveto Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's been a pleasure, as always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it mean that his evidence will be interposed on Monday by Veselinovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we can continue his evidence and finish it on Monday and then have Mr. Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's correct. Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There seems to be some miscommunication, or it is the understanding of the VWS that the Defence informed that he is due to testify next week, not today. So the upshot is that he's not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Mr. President. I'll look into how that happened. But in the meantime we will start with Mr. Veselinovic on Monday and then have Mr. Kovacevic after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, unless there is any matters to be raised, the hearing is adjourned.
